items.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
items.summary: Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.
items.content:
Image caption, OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney
By Lana Lam   and   Simon Atkinson ,  Australia producer
OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.
The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.
"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.
Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.
Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.
An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.
When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.
"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.
"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."
Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.
"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."
OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.
The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.
Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.
This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.
The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".
"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."
Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.
"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.
The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.
An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.
"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.
Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

items.content:
Protests in Lyon on Tuesday. Photograph: Olivier Chassignole/AFP/Getty Images
Protests in Lyon on Tuesday. Photograph: Olivier Chassignole/AFP/Getty Images
‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing
Unprecedented protests that began in low-income suburb are turning ugly, with investigations under way into police brutality
Europe live: latest updates from protests in France
B efore dawn on Tuesday outside the Lycée Sophie-Germain in central Paris , hundreds of teenagers dragged wheelie bins, metal barriers and shopping trolleys to build a barricade outside the front door of their secondary school.
Climbing to the top of the piles of bins, pupils held banners calling for more funding and greater equality in French schools.
But they were also protesting against French riot police, who have been accused by human rights groups of using disproportionate force against children in what is fast becoming the biggest youth protest movement in decades .
“Everyone hates the police,” chanted a group of 15- and 16-year-olds. At least 215 teenagers, 715 police officers and 85 teaching staff have been injured in clashes in recent days, according to the government.
“We’re teenagers with wheelie bins, and the police have heavy weapons, it’s totally mismatched,” said Livia, 17, who was studying theatre at a lycée in northern Paris and did not want her real name published.
“The police are extremely violent in France . This is state violence and it’s horrible seeing police allowed to target children. It’s important to remember this is institutionalised violence, it’s planned and deliberate.”
A large student protest in Nantes on Tuesday. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters Ten investigations into possible police brutality are under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including one 15-year-old who lost his hand , another who lost his eye and a boy whose jaw and teeth were shattered, leaving him, as his mother said, barely able to eat with a straw in hospital.
“The policing is catastrophic, people have been mutilated by weapons – one boy has lost an eye – it’s horrible,” said Lily, 17 (not her real name), who was studying social sciences in her final year of school and demonstrating for more funding in what she called a discriminatory education system that left poorer children behind.
“My parents support me being on the barricades and at the protests. They’re worried about the policing, but they said they’d come and get me from the police station if I was arrested.”
French riot police in Lyon on Tuesday. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters Teenagers nearby held up cardboard signs protesting against the use of teargas and the deployment of riot police.
“A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” read one banner. “Gas rapists, not children,” said another sign in reference to calls for tougher laws against sexual violence. Another banner read: “Not here to riot.”
The unprecedented protest movement that began outside one school in a low-income Paris suburb has spread across the country, taking the government by surprise.
Hundreds of high schools have been barricaded and forced to close as pupils protest against teacher shortages, crumbling buildings and overcrowded classes.
The justice ministry said 5,060 people had been arrested ⁠since the protests began, 87% of them minors. More than 1,800 people had been prosecuted, ​including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without specifying ​the crimes. It said 790 cases had been ​dismissed. The government said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked.
“In more than 20 years of teaching, I’ve never seen protests this big,” said one teacher at Sophie-Germain high school who planned to join the Paris demonstration on Tuesday afternoon.
“The students in central Paris have shown a great sense of solidarity with those in the Paris suburbs who face much worse conditions in their schools. There’s a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers that flies in the face of the notion that we live in an era of selfishness. No one knows how long this will go on for.”
A protester in Montpellier on Friday. Photograph: Horcajuelo Guillaume/EPA Tens of thousands of students, trade unionists and parents were expected to march in support of the protests across France on Tuesday afternoon, including in Paris, Toulouse, Nice and Bordeaux, with riot police on alert.
Isabella, 16, said she had the backing of her parents, who work in film and music.
“Young people have been teargassed for doing nothing but trying to express their opinion,” she said.
“Everybody told us that school was the great leveller, but today that is not the case at all. A teenager in the banlieue [suburbs] of Paris is never going to have the same opportunities as a student from the city centre. That’s why we’re here today.”
Lionel, 17, who was in his final year at school and hoped to study English at university, said: “The aim isn’t to riot or smash things up, we just want to protest peacefully.”
Demonstrations in Paris on Tuesday. Photograph: Tom Nicholson/Reuters Teenagers also chanted songs against Marine Le Pen , the far-right, anti-immigration candidate in the 2027 presidential election, who is high in the polls as Emmanuel Macron steps down after a decade in office.
Many teenagers were worried about the election. “We’re also protesting against the growth of the far right,” said Aislinn.
Justine, 17, who had been at the barricade since before dawn, said she hoped the protest would continue and grow into a “massive” movement.
“For years, there has been a mental health crisis among young people in France and anger at rundown schools and the stresses of the education system. We need the government to listen to us and make radical change.”
Maya, an 18-year-old sports science student, had spent two days on a barricade at her university building in Bobigny in solidarity with school students, and joined the Paris protest march on Tuesday.
She had attended high school in Drancy in Seine-Saint-Denis outside Paris, in a school she said had mould on the walls, not enough chairs for class and absent teachers who often were not replaced.
“It’s only when we spoke to other students at university who came from different types of schools in the countryside or city centres that we realised our experience was so different and that there was a real injustice to the conditions we had to learn in,” she said.
Protests in Lyon on Tuesday. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters Julie, 46, a self-employed parent of two high schoolchildren from Levallois, in the west of Paris, had joined her husband to accompany her sons to the Paris march.
She said: “We’re here to support our children but also to protect them from what is going on with the police and the violence we’ve seen with the police these last few days. We’ve seen our own child teargassed many times in front of his school … it’s unbelievable.”

items.content:
Delegates at the National Conservatism Conference in Brussels, on 16 April 2024. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images
Delegates at the National Conservatism Conference in Brussels, on 16 April 2024. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images
US, Israeli and European far-right figures to gather for conference in Israel
Trump’s counter-terrorism ‘czar’, Sebastian Gorka, was scheduled to speak at conference but White House says he will no longer attend
A National Conservatism (NatCon) conference beginning today in Jerusalem advertises a talk from the Trump administration’s anti-terrorism czar alongside speeches from far-right Israeli politicians, European figures who have faced disciplinary action over alleged antisemitism, and Christian nationalist and far-right figures from the United States.
The Jerusalem event is perhaps the most significant recent gathering to feature large contingents of Israeli nationalists alongside Christian nationalists and far-right European nationalists from a milieu sometimes shadowed by accusations of antisemitism.
Sebastian Gorka, a senior White House official whose May anti-terrorism strategy promised to target and neutralise groups “whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist”, was scheduled to speak at the Jerusalem event, and his presence is still advertised on the website.
But when the Guardian contacted the White House for comment on Gorka’s attendance at the conference, a spokesperson advised that he would no longer be attending due to a scheduling conflict, and that he had condemned Hamas’s 7 October attack on Israel.
Sebastian Gorka at the AmericaFest 2024 conference, sponsored by conservative group Turning Point in Phoenix, Arizona, on 20 December 2024. Photograph: Cheney Orr/Reuters From Israel, the program lists Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, self-declared “fascist homophobe” and internationally sanctioned extremist, and Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu, who in 2023 called for an atom bomb to be dropped on Gaza and was earlier ordered to face disciplinary proceedings for racist incitement against Palestinians.
From Europe come Hans-Georg Maaßen, who once led Germany’s domestic intelligence agency but in 2023 faced an expulsion attempt by his then party, the CDU, for “statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues”, and Austria’s Harald Vilimsky, whose far-right Freedom party has been subject to a policy of non-engagement by Israel’s own government.
According to Israeli media reports, Vilimsky has played a key role in building a rapprochement between the Freedom party – whose first two leaders after its founding in 1956 were former SS officers – and Tel Aviv. He has visited the country repeatedly and in January reportedly led a European delegation to the country that was received by Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, despite criticism from Austria’s own Jewish community.
In a statement, Maaßen wrote: “I firmly reject the claim that I made ‘statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues’. This deliberately vague wording was never a concrete accusation but a politically motivated label, designed to damage my reputation and to discredit critics of the political mainstream of the time,” Vilimsky was also contacted for comment.
Hans-Georg Maaßen, former head of the Germany domestic intelligence service takes part in a constituency meeting of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) district associations in Suhl, eastern Germany, on 30 April 2021. Photograph: Jens Schlueter/AFP/Getty Images The American contingent includes William Wolfe, a self-described Christian nationalist who has called for “mass deportations, denaturalizations, and remigration” to preserve a white Christian majority, and Jonathan Keeperman, the publisher unmasked by the Guardian in 2024 as the man behind the far-right internet persona “L0m3z”.
Keeperman did not address questions sent to him when asked for comment. Wolfe did not respond directly to questions on his attendance at NatCon, instead sending personal insults.
Dr Brendan McGeever, co-director of Birkbeck University’s Institute for the Study of Antisemitism , said: “Many attendees at NatCon view Israel not just as an ally but as an embodiment of the exclusionary ethnostate they wish to establish. National Conservatism sees in Israel a blueprint for the realization of a white, Christian nation built on racialized exclusion, while far-right Israeli attenders at NatCon often argue that partnering with white Christian nationalists is the best way to protect Israel. It is racism that binds these forces together.”
Attenders will also share a stage with high-profile conservatives including the Heritage Foundation president, Kevin Roberts , and former deputy national security adviser Victoria Coates , who is now vice-president at Heritage’s Davis Institute for National Security and Foreign Policy.
The Guardian contacted Heritage with questions about their attendance at NatCon.
Last October Roberts defended Tucker Carlson after the broadcaster gave a friendly interview to the white nationalist and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, saying in a video that “the venomous coalition attacking him are sowing division”. He later called the phrase “a terrible choice of words”, and said he and Heritage would speak out against antisemitism. In July a Heritage spokesperson said the thinktank’s “record opposing antisemitism is long, consistent and public”. In May, Heritage elected the Israeli nationalist and rightwing intellectual Yoram Hazony to its board.
Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts introduces former vice-president Mike Pence during an event to promote his new book at the conservative thinktank on 19 October 2022 in Washington. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Roberts and Wolfe are among the NatCon Jerusalem attenders singled out last month by the evangelical conservative commentator Erick Erickson, in a broadside against “a group of white guys” who “have subtly inserted themselves into conservative institutions and church organizations” and who “to varying degrees … embrace white nationalism, antisemitism”.
Erickson’s principal target was the shampoo tycoon and would-be “warlord” Charles Haywood, the subject of extensive previous reporting in the Guardian, but he also singled out Heritage fellow Scott Yenor , another Jerusalem speaker. He was supported in his efforts by other NatCon attenders, including the writer Rod Dreher.
The Guardian contacted Haywood and Erickson for comment.
Matthew Taylor, a senior visiting fellow at the Georgetown Center for Faith and Justice and author of the new book Defying Tyrants , said: “I think they were trying to find a way to kind of carve out a version of Christian nationalism that could synchronize with kind of European and Israeli politics … and I think what they’re discovering is kind of the impossibility of that.”
He added: “[Hazony is] running up against the limits of that project because the reality is that you can’t simply stir up abstract Christian nationalism. One side of the Christian nationalist coalition is very aligned with Israel, is very Christian Zionist, the other side is leaning hard into this antisemitic impulse.”
The gathering is the latest in a series of NatCon conferences held in the United States and abroad since 2019 by the Edmund Burke Foundation , whose founder is Hazony.
The conferences are high-profile gatherings of the international national conservative movement, which scholars describe as the most influential strand of an anti-liberal “New Right” .
Past NatCons have featured JD Vance , Viktor Orbán, Giorgia Meloni and Nigel Farage , and have drawn accusations of racism and extremism since a speaker at the first Washington conference argued for an immigration policy of “more whites and fewer nonwhites”. Conference organizer Hazony, reportedly said at that time that the speaker’s views were “legitimate and should be heard and debated”. In 2024 a Brussels mayor ordered police to shut the event down before a court overturned him.
Gorka is listed for a 7 October plenary titled “The Meaning of October 7”, alongside Israel’s diaspora affairs minister, Amichai Chikli, and the former Polish president Andrzej Duda. The Guardian previously reported on a video in which Gorka offered Israeli leaders advice on Hamas: “Kill every single one of them. God bless Israel. God bless Judeo-Christian civilisation.”
In August 2024 Smotrich said of Gaza: “Nobody will let us cause 2 million civilians to die of hunger, even though it might be justified and moral, until our hostages are returned.” Britain sanctioned him on 10 June 2025, acting with Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway. It held him responsible for “inciting, promoting and/or supporting” abuses, “in particular acts of aggression and violence against Palestinian individuals in the West Bank”.
Rabbi Eliyahu, who for decades has served as chief rabbi of Safed, a public office in Israel, remarked of Palestinians in Gaza in a lecture his office posted to YouTube in November 2023, “Drop an atom [bomb] on them? It’s an option,” he said . The disciplinary hearing Israel’s high court ordered in 2020 was reportedly not held until June 2024, and its outcome kept from the public.
The conference’s co-sponsors include the Sovereignty Movement and Regavim, the organisation Smotrich founded . The ultranationalist Israeli television news outlet Channel 14 says it is producing the event with Hazony’s foundation and his Herzl Institute. The conference website does not currently list the channel as a partner.
One panel is titled “Immigration and Cultural Replacement”. Maaßen’s talk is billed as “Why Elites Embrace Mass Migration as a Tool of Cultural, Racial, and Political Transformation”. A fellow panelist, Nathan Pinkoski of the Center for Renewing America , wrote the introduction to a 2025 edition of The Camp of the Saints, a novel Dreher at one time called “ racist ”. Dreher appears to have since softened that view.
Vilimsky reportedly told a Budapest conference in April 2024: “We do not want Mohammed to become the most common name in our countries.” He is listed for a NatCon plenary on 7 October.
Gideon Sa’ar, the foreign minister, who last month welcomed a speech by the FPÖ leader, Herbert Kickl, at a Strasbourg event Vilimsky organised with Likud, as making possible “a substantive, open and sincere dialogue” despite the ongoing disengagement, is listed for the conference dinner on 6 October.
Wolfe told a Texas audience in February: “My boys all look like me. And I want my children to grow up in a country where they’re not minorities.” He has called Erickson’s essay “a call for the assassination of a group of conservative Christians”. His conference bio says he served at the state department and the Pentagon in the first Trump administration.
As previously reported in the Guardian Haywood’s private foundation gave the Edmund Burke Foundation, which organizes the NatCon conferences, $25,000 for “general operations” in the year to June 2023, its tax filing shows.
Hazony’s former communications director was among the Jewish conservatives who criticised him in January, after he blamed an “antisemitism-industrial complex” for failing to make the case against Tucker Carlson. He has since refused Carlson a speaking slot in Jerusalem, and on 28 September called the broadcaster’s show “the leading clearinghouse for antisemitism on the political Right in America”.
Taylor, the religion scholar, said: “[Hazony is] still trying to play an older game of drawing boundary lines and saying, oh, there is an antisemitic far right that is the fringe that we have to cut off … But Tucker Carlson is not [fringe]. Tucker Carlson is about as mainstream today in rightwing politics as you can get.”
The Guardian contacted the Carlson Network’s press office for comment.
McGeever, the antisemitism scholar, wrote: “Yoram Hazony may express bewilderment about this surge of antisemitism, but it is baked into the very political alliances he has forged. His allies have repeatedly promoted ideas about ‘globalist elites’ and ‘secret cabals’ which utilize the same structural logic of antisemitic conspiracy theories.”
The conference runs from 6 to 8 October at Jerusalem’s International Convention Center.

items.title: Nigeria mourns 25 killed as military plane crashes into swamp
items.summary: President Bola Tinubu describes the crash as a "painful moment" for the military and the entire nation.
items.content:
Image caption, Some wreckage was recovered from the water
By Makuochi Okafor ,  BBC Africa ,  Reporting from Lagos   and   Basillioh Rukanga
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 25 people.
Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo on Monday said 32 people had died but on Tuesday the Air Force clarified that 25 people had been killed - five crew and 20 passengers.
Authorities say the plane was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it came down in a swamp near a naval base on Monday morning. After reaching the site, the aircraft was found to be submerged under water, officials said.
A resident told the BBC that clothes and shoes had been found at the site. Smoke could be seen rising from the area.
It is the deadliest crash involving a Nigerian military aircraft since 1992.
The Nigerian Air Force has released the names of those killed, showing that 19 of those on board were military personnel.
Tinubu offered his deepest condolences to those killed and has ordered a full investigation.
The president also ordered national flags to be flown at half-mast across the country as a mark of respect for those who died.
"This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," Tinubu said.
"Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten," he added.
The aviation minister earlier said he had been informed "of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today".
Keyamo said "efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive" before subsequent confirmation that it had crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo state.
The crashed plane, described as an ATR-42 aircraft, carries between 30 and 50 passengers, according to its manufacturers.
Image caption, Officials from Ondo state visited the site of the crash
Tinubu has ordered the Air Force to immediately begin a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to help prevent similar incidents in the future.
The Nigerian Air Force plays a key role in the country's military operations, including efforts to tackle armed groups and insecurity in several parts of the country.
In May 2021, Nigeria's army chief, Lt-Gen Ibrahim Attahiru, was killed in a plane crash alongside 10 other officers in the north-western state of Kaduna amid bad weather.
In February of the same year, seven people died after a military plane crashed short of a runway in the capital Abuja.

items.content:
Nvidia ( NVDA +0.14% ) and Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD +2.80% ) are seeing booming demand for graphics processing units (GPUs) . The consensus estimate has both companies growing revenue roughly 90% and 45%, respectively, this year. But you don't have to choose between winners and losers in this GPU rivalry.
Every chip still has to be designed, printed, and paired with fast memory before it can train or run an AI model. ASML ( ASML -1.39% ) , Synopsys ( SNPS +3.42% ) , and Micron Technology ( MU -1.73% ) provide these essential steps in the chipmaking process, offering investors another way to ride the growing demand across the chip industry.
ASML supplies the extreme ultraviolet lithography systems that print circuit patterns on chips. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing builds Nvidia and AMD GPUs, and it buys that equipment from ASML. Without those tools, the GPUs do not get made.
Management sees surging demand for AI chips, prompting customers to add manufacturing capacity. Analysts expect full-year 2026 sales to grow 32% over 2025, then another 27% in 2027. Order momentum was "extremely strong" in the first half of 2026, driving backlog growth across a broad mix of customers.
The shares trade at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 57 as of Oct. 1, 2026. That valuation leaves downside risk if growth stalls. However, CEO Christophe Fouquet said on the second-quarter earnings call that the company has demand visibility extending several years.
In 2027 estimates, though, the multiple falls to 30 times earnings. Analysts expect 31% annualized earnings growth, a P/E-to-growth (PEG) ratio of about 1.0. That valuation leaves room for upside as the semiconductor industry continues to grow.

Synopsys is a leading supplier of electronic design automation (EDA), the software Nvidia and AMD use to design chips before being sent to TSMC. Growth is accelerating as AI and high-performance compute customers run more designs.
Revenue surged 42% year over year to nearly $2.5 billion in the fiscal third quarter of 2026. It converts that revenue into robust profits, earning an adjusted operating margin of 41.6%. A $10.9 billion backlog indicates more growth ahead.
AMD designed its Instinct MI4155X AI GPU with Synopsys' 3DIC Compiler. Synopsys offers innovation that sets it apart in a competitive industry. Its Multiphysics Fusion is the only product that integrates thermal analysis into the design flow, and Nvidia, Cisco Systems , MediaTek, and Samsung Foundry have validated it.
Revenue has grown steadily over the past 10 years, including during the 2022 chip industry downturn. Its consistent revenue growth reflects recurring software licenses that smooth out its revenue generation. The stock still looks like a solid buy, trading at a forward P/E of 28 on 2027 estimates, against expected annualized earnings growth of 22%.
$1.2T Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Micron supplies DRAM and NAND flash memory for high-speed data retrieval and storage in AI data centers. Advanced versions are co-packaged with Nvidia and AMD GPUs, so a stronger GPU cycle pulls memory with it. Micron is also the only U.S.-based supplier of high bandwidth memory, which makes it a natural partner for both.
Fiscal 2026 revenue hit a record $133 billion, up 256% from the prior year. Gross margin expanded 40 percentage points to 81% for the year as a supply shortage lifted memory prices and profits.
Management expects higher gross margins in fiscal 2027, though only a moderate rise in prices. Selling prices are the key risk. Long-term custom agreements account for over 35% of revenue through 2030, leaving a large share exposed to pricing swings.
Management still expects fiscal 2027 to be another record year. Micron is collaborating with Nvidia on the first custom HBM4E memory for next-generation GPUs.
Overbuilding supply to meet demand could eventually put pressure on memory prices. The prospect of another downturn in selling prices and earnings is why the market is pricing the stock at a conservative 7 times forward earnings. Still, there could be substantial upside if Micron can sign more customer agreements, thereby extending visibility into future revenue.

items.summary: Nvidia vs. Broadcom: Which AI Chip Stock Is the Better Buy Now?  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Nvidia vs. Broadcom: Which AI Chip Stock Is the Better Buy Now?
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO ) offer two different claims on the AI computing budget. Nvidia sells a broad GPU platform supported by software and integrated systems. Broadcom helps customers build custom accelerators and supplies networking alongside a substantial software business. An investor choosing between them needs to decide which company can retain more cash as customers seek cheaper computing.
At the October 5 close, their trailing cash-flow valuations were close enough that the business differences matter more than a small discount. My preference is Nvidia, provided its software advantage continues to protect margins and its infrastructure guarantees do not absorb that benefit. Broadcom becomes more compelling if custom chips gain share while financing support at both companies stays contained.
The custom-chip choice extends beyond these two stocks. Our Broadcom-versus-Marvell comparison examines how much investors are paying for current cash generation versus later customer ramps .
Nvidia vs. Broadcom: Which AI Chip Stock Is the Better Buy Now? Nvidia's margin is the advantage custom chips must erode
Nvidia's August 26 report showed revenue of $96.2 billion for the quarter ended July 26, up 106% year over year. Its 75% GAAP gross margin indicates that buyers were still paying well above the company's production costs. CUDA's libraries, development tools and compatibility with established applications help explain the attraction: changing hardware can also require engineering work and performance validation. That creates a cost of switching beyond the processor's purchase price.
The bullish case is that customers keep valuing that flexibility as models and workloads change. Nvidia can earn from a platform usable across many buyers rather than depend on the success of one customer's chip design. The bearish case is that large customers eventually find enough predictable work to justify specialized alternatives. Custom silicon need not replace every GPU to limit Nvidia's pricing power on the workloads where substitution is economical.
Deployment constraints can also delay demand even when the computing opportunity remains attractive. Our analysis of Nvidia's flexible AI factory asks which operating test extra funding alone cannot solve . Power availability and useful computing output belong in the demand assessment alongside a customer's announced budget.
Historical ownership gives Nvidia broader long-side participation: Insider Monkey's hedge fund database recorded 285 holders in Q2 2026, up from 275 in Q1. Fisher Asset Management held 90,935,947 shares after increasing its position about 3%. Those positions predate the August results. At the September 15 settlement, 294,225,803 shares were sold short, about 1.27% of float, giving limited support for a thesis built around crowded short positioning.
Broadcom's faster AI growth comes with a narrower customer base
Broadcom's September 2 results reported $29.6 billion of quarterly revenue, up 86%, for the period ended August 2. AI semiconductor revenue rose 221% to $16.7 billion. That is the strongest operating argument for choosing Broadcom: customers pursuing custom computing are already producing substantial sales. Its latest quarter also generated $13.7 billion of free cash flow, equal to 46% of revenue.
Custom designs can build durable engineering relationships, while networking gives Broadcom another way to earn as clusters expand. Infrastructure software supplied $8.75 billion of quarterly revenue. It offers a separate profit pool, although license revenue means the segment's sales are not uniformly recurring subscriptions. The investment case depends on retained margins and collections as much as the announced chip opportunity.
Concentration makes those economics more sensitive to a few buyers. Broadcom's five largest end customers accounted for 55% of quarterly revenue. A large program can support efficient development, but a buyer with alternatives can bargain for a greater share of the savings. Our dividend analysis tests how much protection today's cash coverage provides when those customers gain negotiating power .
The financing risk also deserves a place in the comparison. Broadcom disclosed a maximum potential liability of about $29 billion under a five-year customer-lease backstop upon deployment of all relevant AI racks. No amounts had been paid, and the backstop's fair value was immaterial. For scale, that contingent maximum equals nearly three-quarters of its $39.4 billion annual trailing free cash flow, although the potential obligations extend across several years. A customer default and weaker equipment resale values could make financing support costly just when demand deteriorates.
Broadcom's hedge-fund-holder count fell to 170 in Q2 2026 from 173 in Q1. Fisher Asset Management increased its share position about 3% to 15,131,673. The manager increased both holdings while the aggregate holder counts moved differently. These disclosures describe historical exposure; the operating and valuation comparison must supply the investment judgment.
Similar cash-flow prices leave little room for complacency
At closing prices of $239.09 for Nvidia and $362.51 for Broadcom on October 5, the stocks traded at about 45.6 and 44.0 times trailing free cash flow, respectively. Both measures use equity value divided by trailing operating cash flow less capital expenditure, through July 26 for Nvidia and August 2 for Broadcom. Nvidia's premium was only about 4%. Broadcom's rapid AI growth could justify that small valuation advantage. Its customer concentration qualifies the bargain, while contingent financing exposure requires scrutiny at both companies.
The cash measure also has limits. It adds back stock compensation, includes interest and can fluctuate with working capital. It does not deduct every acquisition or strategic investment. Nvidia's capital-expenditure figure includes intangible-asset purchases but excludes equipment and intangible-asset principal payments, unlike the company's own free-cash-flow definition.
Nvidia's latest quarterly filing also disclosed guarantees signed in August, capped at $105 billion, supporting an OpenAI affiliate's infrastructure with SB Energy. Exposure generally begins as each lease commences, with the first data centers expected to be placed in service in fiscal 2029. Payments depend on specified tenant defaults; guaranteed amounts decline over 20-year leases and cover defined portions of lease and power payments. The cap is not current debt or an expected loss. Broadcom's five-year rack backstop and Nvidia's longer infrastructure guarantees have different assets, remedies and timing; their headline maximums cannot establish which stock has the safer financing profile.
Supply obligations add another demand risk. Nvidia disclosed $279 billion of supply and capacity commitments across future fiscal years, some adjustable or cancelable at a cost. Broadcom disclosed $126.8 billion of unconditional purchase commitments, mainly inventory. Neither total is an immediate cash bill, but slower customer spending could leave commitments harder to absorb.
An illustrative multiple contraction shows the hurdle facing both stocks. If a 45-times cash-flow valuation fell to 30 times, cash flow would need to rise 50% just to preserve the same equity value, assuming no change in share count. Over two years, that requires growth of about 22.5% annually before providing capital appreciation. This is a sensitivity, not a forecast or a fair-value estimate.
Nvidia seems preferable at this relatively small premium because its broad software platform gives it a stronger route to retaining pricing across changing workloads. That judgment would weaken if custom chips took enough economically attractive work to reduce Nvidia's margins while Broadcom sustained superior cash-flow growth, or if Nvidia's guarantee payments consumed the cash benefit of its platform. Broadcom would then offer the better exposure, provided its own financing commitments remained manageable. For now, the decisive evidence is cash growth after the costs of winning and funding demand, with continued margin strength making Nvidia my preferred stock.
While we acknowledge the potential of NVDA and AVGO as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Jim Cramer’s AI stock picks: Meta, Microsoft and more
Jim Cramer said established tech giants with strong businesses and multiple ways to benefit from AI are some of the best places to invest in the boom.
He remains diversified but is overweight AI, arguing those stocks offer more opportunities for growth as higher rates weigh on much of the rest of the market.
AI-related stocks give you the most opportunity for something to go right, says Jim Cramer
CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that some of the best ways to invest in the artificial intelligence boom are established tech giants with multiple opportunities to capitalize on the technology.
The " Mad Money " host acknowledged concerns about stretched AI valuations and comparisons with the dotcom bubble. Rather than backing away from a trade that continues to drive much of the market's gains , Cramer said he favors blue-chip companies with strong businesses and management teams that can find new ways to benefit from AI.
"Because I think that a lot of things can possibly go right, I want to stick with the AI data center plays," Cramer said.
He pointed to Meta and Microsoft as two examples. Cramer's CNBC Investing Club owns both stocks.
While Meta shares had a rocky start to 2026, Cramer said he trusted CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team to figure out how to monetize its AI spending, which the Facebook and Instagram parent is expected to do with Muse . The stock now trades around $738.
"I didn't think, 'what a bunch of chowderheads, they don't have anything AI,'" Cramer said. "I thought that Mark Zuckerberg and his dream team are brilliant and they'll figure something out."
Cramer had a similar view of Microsoft when shares traded at a 52-week low of $350 in June. "I didn't think their best times were behind them," Cramer said, despite at times expressing frustration in the stock's performance. Ultimately, though, Cramer retained the Club's shares because of his trust in the veteran leadership team of CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood.
"I thought, 'They're going to figure out this Copilot, and with their Azure web services business they're going to make a ton of money.'" Shares now trade around $529, as the market has grown more confident in Microsoft's plan for Copilot. Also, in late July, the performance and guidance for Azure also surpassed Wall Street expectations , leading to a stock rally.
Cramer also highlighted Advanced Micro Devices and Intel in semiconductors, Marvell Technology in chips and fiber, and CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks in cybersecurity.
The strategy looks particularly attractive to Cramer as higher interest rates make growth harder to find elsewhere. AI-related companies, by contrast, are among the relatively few businesses that can continue delivering strong growth in this environment, he said.
"When I query about 80% of the S&P 500 about what can possibly go right, I can't even think of anything for most of them," Cramer said. "Sure, that can change when the war ends. Until then, though, the AI-related stocks give you the most opportunity for something to go right."
That doesn't mean the AI trade is without risk. Cramer acknowledged that enthusiasm can become excessive. He also stressed, "I want to be diversified, and I certainly run a diversified" portfolio for the Investing Club.

items.content:
Not Nvidia. Not Micron. If I Could Buy and Hold Only 1 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chip Stock Through 2030, It Would be This One.
Every GPU that powers a model training cluster has to be built somewhere, and that somewhere is almost always a fab operated by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM). Taiwan Semi does not design the artificial intelligence (AI) chips that get the headlines. Instead, the company manufactures them at nodes no one else can reliably hit at scale.
That quiet competitive advantage has turned TSMC into the physical backbone of the AI infrastructure buildout. Nevertheless, the conversation still seems to start and end with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD), or Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). The foundry that is actually printing the silicon rarely gets the same amount of airtime.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
This gap is strange once you understand how the AI chip stack works. While designers continue to fight over architecture and software, the constraint that decides how many of those designs actually ship is advanced-node capacity -- and TSMC owns most of that market.
Image source: Getty Images. The foundry actually supporting the AI chip stack
Nvidia and AMD design GPUs while Micron builds memory solutions layered alongside these chips. None of these companies do all of the manufacturing work to bring their products to life, however. TSMC holds roughly 73% of the pure-play foundry market as measured by revenue and reportedly closer to 90% of the market for the most advanced nodes.
For years, Apple was credited as TSMC's largest customer. However, Nvidia took over that title earlier this year. This shift directly tracks the AI infrastructure cycle. High-performance computing, the area that covers AI accelerators and related server silicon, has become Taiwan Semi's core growth engine.
The company's management points to AI-accelerator revenue compounding in the mid-to-high 50% range through the end of the decade, and lifted its longer-term company revenue growth outlook toward at least 25%.
While competition from Samsung and Intel exist, both companies are spending heavily on scaling foundry operations and neither company is yet to close the gap on the yield and volume at nodes Nvidia and AMD actually need for current and next-generation accelerators.
TSMC's financial growth supports the idea that the AI infrastructure supercycle is more than a temporary surge. Full-year 2025 revenue reached about $122 billion, up nearly 36% year over year. Meanwhile, gross margin climbed to 60% from 56% percent the year before. Through the first half of 2026, Taiwan Semi's revenue grew 37% year over year to $76.1 billion while while gross margin expanded into the mid-60% range, underscoring the level of pricing power the company commands right now.
The company is also spending heavily on capital expenditures (capex) to help stay ahead of demand. Rising infrastructure spend might look expensive in any single year, but over a multi-year AI buildout it is what keeps the company's moat intact. Customers cannot easily dual-source manufacturing for leading edge nodes. This makes Taiwan Semi's revenue and profit tailwinds tied to the duration of the infrastructure supercycle itself rather than to one specific product launch.
The chart below illustrates how investors are treating TSMC as a picks-and-shovels name that should trade at a discount to some of the primary chip designers. Trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) puts the stock near 34 times, which looks rich upon first glance. But on a forward P/E basis, Taiwan Semi is a different story. While the company's forward P/E of 28 is not a deep-value multiple per se, it is also not stretched against a company still expected to grow revenue by a high double-digit percent range and compound earnings as margins hold.
Nvidia and AMD capture more of the narrative premium because their products are visible. For the time being, Micron will ride the memory upcycle that AI also requires. Taiwan Semi sits underneath all of them.
While geopolitical risk around Taiwan is an obvious factor to consider, in addition to the cost of building fabs here in the U.S., they do not erase a foundry position that remains the hardest part of the AI supply chain to replicate. On a forward earnings valuation basis, I think TSMC stock still looks like a strong candidate to buy and hold throughout the AI infrastructure era.

items.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
items.summary: The deal is expected to alter the entertainment and news industries but could it mean higher prices for consumers?
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you
By Francisco Velasquez ,  Business reporter ,  Reporting from New York   and   Regan Morris ,  Reporting from California
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.
Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.
Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.
Image caption, HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya
Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.
Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time.
While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability .
The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.
Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal.
Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come.
While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes".
Image caption, Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance
As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger , Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.
For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.
That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas.
The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.
If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.
Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.
"Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said.
"Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".
Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.
As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.
Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.
Image caption, Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA
For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground.
Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.
Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken".
"It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."
A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.
The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.
Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities".
She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."
Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.
"Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added.
Image caption, CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building
To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.
The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.
Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.
Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.
Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.
Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.
Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless".
"The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said.
Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said.

items.content:
Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video under six-year deal
Amazon's Prime Video will become the exclusive global home of the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal beginning in 2027.
The Emmys will stream live and free in more than 240 countries and territories, with no Prime subscription required.
The agreement ends the Emmys' long-running broadcast network rotation among ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC.
An Emmy statue is seen on the red carpet ahead of the 74th Emmy Awards at the Microsoft Theater in Los Angeles, California, on Sept. 12, 2022.
The Emmy Awards will leave its long-running broadcast network rotation for Amazon Prime Video in 2027 under a six-year exclusive global streaming deal, the e-commerce giant and the Television Academy announced on Tuesday.
Under the agreement, Prime Video will stream the annual awards honoring the best in TV for free to all audiences, including nonsubscribers, in more than 240 countries and territories.
Prime Video's rights to the Emmys will begin with the 2027 ceremony. NBC, owned by Comcast , aired the 2026 ceremony on Sept. 14.
In the release, Prime Video was named as the "permanent home" for the Emmys, in contrast to the rotating agreement in place years prior.
The switch ends the traditional "wheel-deal" setup to broadcast the awards, where ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox took turns hosting the Emmys each year. The system has been in place since at least 1994 , with the most recent eight-year contract expiring this year.
"Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement.
"Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year," he said.
The decision to move the 70-plus-year-old awards show to streaming reflects a broader trend in a shifting media landscape as Americans continue to ditch broadcast and cable TV for streaming service subscriptions. Streaming services have pushed further into live events in recent years, securing entertainment and sports rights alongside broadcast networks, and even winning rights that were previously exclusive to networks.
In December 2025, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal with Alphabet's YouTube and YouTube TV for media rights to the Oscars, taking over from ABC in 2029. Netflix has exclusively aired the SAG Awards since 2024.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), says the Pentagon blocked him from a key U.S. military base in Qatar while he traveling in the Middle East, accusing the Trump administration of trying to hide damage caused by the Iran war.
Murphy, who traveled to Doha, Qatar, and later Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, as part of a congressional delegation, said he attempted to visit the Al Udeid Air Base — the largest U.S. base in the region that Iran has repeatedly attacked since the war began in late February.
Prior to the trip, Murphy said he wanted “to see firsthand the impact of the Iran War, the damage it’s caused to our facilities in the region, and how it’s harmed our relationships with partners in the region.”
But after being barred from visiting Al Udeid, Murphy said, “There is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people,” as reported by Reuters .
He also said that the Defense Department refused to set up a briefing for him on the war while he was in the region.
“I’ve never encountered anything like this in my time in the Senate and it’s part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to,” Murphy added.
Asked about Murphy’s accusations, a senior Pentagon official told The Hill that the senator’s office was informed prior to his trip to the Middle East that he would not receive Defense Department support to access Al Udeid, pointing to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s March directive on travel restrictions in the region.
“That decision was communicated in advance by the Office of the Secretary of War for Legislative Affairs. The Department applies the Secretary’s guidance evenly,” the official said in a statement.
Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the first Democratic lawmaker to visit the region since the start of the Iran war, made clear that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had helped make the trip possible and arranged meetings with senior Gulf officials.
But the Connecticut senator has called out President Trump for having no clear plan to end the conflict, which now has a price tag of more than $45 billion.
The Pentagon also continues to face scrutiny over its opacity about the mounting toll from the conflict, which has dragged on for more than seven months.
The U.S. military has placed the number of service members who have died in the Middle East since the start of the conflict at 19. Last month, however, The Washington Post reported that there are at least 23 military fatalities.
“[Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth has been hiding the cost of the war, the extent of its damages, and the loss of American life from the public and from Congress,” Murphy said prior to the trip.

items.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
items.summary: The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you
Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape.
The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers.
It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.
The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network.
Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings to add to its existing catalogue of hit franchises which includes Indiana Jones, Mission: Impossible and Shrek.
The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover.
Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry.
"From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said.
Films and streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
Asked about the merger after it had been finalised, US President Donald Trump described the deal as "great".
"They're terrific people and it's going to be a great company," he said.
Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive.
Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology.
Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News.
Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content.
Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation".
"While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said the company has high debts at a time when interest rates are high.
"The combined entity, now called Skydance, needs to cut costs and make bigger profits to be able to get the debt down to more manageable levels," he said.
"The fact Tom Cruise movie Digger, Warner Bros' last release before the merger, has been a major flop is a reminder of how the film industry is not a guaranteed ticket to riches."
While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning.
Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away.
Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide".
US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead .
As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS.
Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount.
Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained.
Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons.
Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours.
The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick.
The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement.
To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films.
As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob.
Paramount also must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising to more than 30% through the following three years.

items.content:
Centalion acquires Haynesville upstream and midstream natural gas assets from Silver Hill Energy Partners
Centalion Group, one of the world's largest independent physical energy trading companies, has acquired a high-quality portfolio of upstream and midstream natural gas assets in Texas and Louisiana from Silver Hill Energy Partners, a leading Texas-based private oil and gas company.
Centalion Group, one of the world's largest independent physical energy trading companies, has acquired a high-quality portfolio of upstream and midstream natural gas assets in Texas and Louisiana from Silver Hill Energy Partners, a leading Texas-based private oil and gas company.
· Current net production of approximately 300 MMft 3 d of natural gas
· Approximately 72,000 net acres strategically located in the core of the Haynesville and Bossier development areas
· Approximately 300 gross operated development locations, which provides meaningful growth and inventory life.
Silver Hill assembled most of the position through strategic acquisitions between late 2021 and mid-2023. Amid exceptional gas-market volatility, it operated up to four rigs and improved development and cost efficiencies. Production increased from under 100 MMft 3 d to more than 300 MMft 3 d, while the company retained hundreds of additional drilling locations. Expanded midstream and saltwater-disposal capacity, long-term gathering and transportation agreements, and flow assurance further supported attractive Gulf Coast trading opportunities.
"After years of disciplined growth and risk management in a fluctuating market, we are thrilled with this outcome and confident our assets will thrive under Centalion's stewardship," said Silver Hill Founder & CEO Kyle D. Miller. "A collaborative and commercial approach from both teams ensured an efficient process, and we look forward to seeing these assets play an increasingly important role for the Haynesville and the broader natural gas market."
This acquisition furthers Centalion's Gulf Coast natural gas strategy, building upon the group's acquisition of assets in the Haynesville earlier this year. On a pro-forma basis, Centalion's Haynesville footprint ranks as one of the largest amongst private operators and positions it as a significant market participant in the US natural gas market.
"This acquisition adds a high-quality, scalable position in the core of Haynesville, with a substantial development runway," said Gary Pedersen, Chairman & CEO of Centalion, "Consistent with the goals of U.S. energy dominance, Centalion will deploy capital to develop U.S. natural resources, generate economic activity in communities, and bolster the domestic energy supply on which households and industries depend."
The transaction marks the continuing success of Centalion's partnership with Western Natural Resources (WNR), led by Heath Mireles. Together with WNR, Centalion intends to execute on an active development program, grow the platform in the basin, and leverage Centalion's integrated Gulf Coast gas capabilities to create long-term value. Strategic Gulf Coast access provides exposure to multiple domestic and liquefied natural gas (LNG) demand points, and the group expects to maximize value by capturing optimization opportunities while leveraging its established marketing and trading capabilities.
Centalion was advised by Greenhill, a Mizuho affiliate, as exclusive financial advisor and Kirkland & Ellis as legal counsel. Silver Hill was advised by Jefferies as exclusive financial advisor and Willkie Farr & Gallagher as legal counsel.
